title: Lazarus, come out (John 11:1–44)
hookLine: Jesus weeps at his friend's tomb, then calls him out

lines: HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.
cards: The phone call nobody wants. Someone you love is sick, you're far away, and you have to decide how fast to come. Now Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem.
Two sisters, Martha and Mary, send word to Jesus about their brother Lazarus, in the King James Bible: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Not our brother. The one you love.
They were close friends. And John says something puzzling: Jesus loved them, and so he stayed where he was two more days. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days.

teach.b: Martha hears he's coming and runs out to meet him on the road, and she's honest: if you had been here, my brother wouldn't have died.

He tells her: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Then Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words: if you had been here.
She's weeping, and everyone with her is weeping. John says he was deeply moved and troubled. Where have you laid him?

Then the shortest verse in the English Bible, two words: "Jesus wept." He knows what he's about to do, and he still weeps. He doesn't skip past the grief to the happy ending; he stands in it with his friends.

The people watching say: "Behold how he loved him!" At the tomb he says, take away the stone, and practical Martha objects: "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." They roll it away anyway.
He prays aloud, then shouts: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man walks out, still wrapped hand and foot in grave clothes, his face bound with a cloth.

teach.h: LOOSE HIM, AND LET HIM GO.
teach.b: The last line is almost tender in its plainness: "Loose him, and let him go." Somebody has to unwrap him.
In John's Gospel this is the last and greatest sign before the cross, and the one that makes the authorities decide he must die.
The name Lazarus comes from the Hebrew Eleazar: God has helped.

how: Many churches read the raising of Lazarus near the end of Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday. Jesus's words I am the resurrection, and the life are read at many Christian funerals.

games.q: you're Martha. Jesus tells you to take away the stone from your brother's tomb. he's been dead four days. what do you say?
o: Lord, by this time he stinketh.
games.why: practical Martha objects: he hath been dead four days. they roll the stone away anyway, and Lazarus comes out.

practice: Is there one thing you haven't let yourself cry about, a loss, a disappointment, a door that closed, a person who's gone, something you moved past too quickly because there was too much to do?
Let it come to mind and stop holding it back; you don't have to force tears, and if they come, let them, because grief isn't a lack of faith. If you pray, you can bring the grief as it is.

wordCard.voice: Lazarus. From the Hebrew Eleazar, God has helped. A friend four days in the tomb, wept over, and called out by name.

orig.note: Greek: he shed tears. A quieter word than the loud wailing of the mourners around him.

carryVoice: Your line: jesus wept. Tomorrow, the last week begins in Jerusalem. Day sixty, and still walking.
